title: Fear and Trembling
author: Søren Kierkegaard
length: Preface + Exordium + Eulogy + Preliminary Expectoration + 3 Problemata + Epilogue (8 chapters)
openingText: Not just in the world of commerce but also in the world of ideas, our age has set up a real auction. Everything can be had so cheap that it becomes a question whether anyone will end up wanting to bid. Every speculative philosopher who conscientiously marks out the significant march of modern thought, every lecturer, tutor, and student — not one stops at doubting everything. They go further. Perhaps it would be untimely and impolite to ask where exactly they are going, but it is surely polite and modest to assume they have already doubted everything, since otherwise it would be a strange way to speak — going further.
about:
Fear and Trembling is Søren Kierkegaard's meditation on Abraham — specifically, on the moment when God commands Abraham to sacrifice his son Isaac. Kierkegaard, writing under the pseudonym Johannes de Silentio, asks how it is possible to call Abraham a "knight of faith" rather than a murderer. The answer he works toward is that faith, real faith, requires a "teleological suspension of the ethical" — a willingness to act on a divine command that violates universal moral law.

Kierkegaard published it in 1843, when he was 30, under a pseudonym he used to keep distance from the work. The book is short — under 200 pages — and reads partly as theology, partly as philosophical drama, partly as the working out of his own broken engagement to a woman named Regine Olsen. It is the founding text of Christian existentialism.

angleCards.title: The teleological suspension of the ethical.
angleCards.text: This is the book's central claim: Abraham's act cannot be justified by any universal moral law. He is not Agamemnon sacrificing Iphigenia for a public cause. He has no external reason to give Sarah, no duty to invoke, no tragedy to perform. Faith, Kierkegaard argues, places the individual in a direct relationship with God that stands above the ethical — not by violating it, but by suspending it from a higher vantage point. Read asking whether any such vantage point is possible, or whether Kierkegaard has simply named a danger.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to trace the concept of the teleological suspension of the ethical through all three Problemata — understanding what Kierkegaard means, why it cannot be reduced to any moral framework, and what this implies for the relationship between religion and ethics.

angleCards.title: Knight of faith vs. knight of infinite resignation.
angleCards.text: Kierkegaard draws a stark contrast between two responses to an impossible loss. The knight of infinite resignation makes the movement of renunciation perfectly — he gives up Isaac, accepts the loss, and finds a kind of tragic dignity in his sacrifice. But he never gets Isaac back. The knight of faith makes one further movement: he gives up Isaac and simultaneously, in the same breath, believes he will receive him back. Only one of these figures returns home. Read asking what the second movement actually requires — and whether you have ever made it.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to read Fear and Trembling for Kierkegaard's distinction between infinite resignation and faith — understanding why resignation is not enough, what the additional movement of faith consists in, and whether the knight of faith is a figure anyone can actually become.

angleCards.title: Against Hegel: faith cannot be mediated.
angleCards.text: The book is a polemic. Its target is a culture — personified in assistant professors, speculative philosophers, and smug clergymen — that has swallowed Hegel and now believes faith is merely an early stage of reason, a preliminary movement that the System has long since surpassed. Kierkegaard's entire effort is to show that Abraham does not belong in the System: he cannot be understood, mediated, or made comfortable. The comic parade of intellectuals in the Preface is already the argument. Read it as an attack on the idea that philosophy has faith covered.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to read Fear and Trembling as a polemic against Hegelian culture — tracking how Kierkegaard uses Abraham's silence and unintelligibility to defeat every attempt at rational mediation, and asking what survives once the System's claim over faith is rejected.

angleCards.title: Johannes de Silentio as a failed witness.
angleCards.text: The narrator is not Kierkegaard. Johannes de Silentio openly admits, from the first page to the last, that he is not a knight of faith — that he cannot make the movement, cannot understand it, can only circle and admire and confess his own incapacity. This is not modesty. It is a structural choice: the book is written from outside faith, by someone who can describe every contour of what he cannot possess. Read asking why Kierkegaard chose this voice, and what it does to the argument that a philosopher cannot even approach this topic in his own name.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to read the pseudonym as an argument — tracing how Johannes de Silentio's admitted incapacity shapes every section of the book, and asking what Kierkegaard accomplishes by refusing to speak in his own name about something he cannot fully inhabit.

cast.name: The Knight of Faith
cast.description: Kierkegaard's highest human type: the person who makes the full movement of resignation — giving up the beloved, accepting the loss absolutely — and then, by virtue of the absurd, believes they will receive it back in this life. Abraham is the supreme instance. The knight of faith looks ordinary from the outside; there is nothing in his bearing that announces the infinite. He is fully at home in the finite and fully oriented toward the infinite at once.

cast.name: The Knight of Infinite Resignation
cast.description: A noble but insufficient figure: one who has made the movement of renunciation fully and perfectly, surrendering the finite in favour of the infinite. He accepts loss without complaint and finds a kind of tragic dignity in it. But he never makes the further movement — he does not believe he will receive the beloved back. He lives in the infinite by giving up the finite, while the knight of faith lives in both simultaneously.

cast.name: The Teleological Suspension of the Ethical
cast.description: The argument that the universal ethical law can be legitimately suspended when a higher telos — the individual's direct relationship with God — demands it. Abraham cannot justify the sacrifice to Sarah, to Isaac, or to any third party, because there is no universal law that covers his situation. He acts on a private absolute duty. Kierkegaard poses this as a genuine possibility, not as an excuse for arbitrary violence, while acknowledging it is also the most dangerous idea he can articulate.

cast.name: The Absurd
cast.description: Not irrationality or nonsense, but the specific content of Abraham's belief: that God can restore what has been absolutely renounced, that the impossible becomes possible, that Isaac will be returned in this life through no logic available to reason. Faith does not abolish the impossibility — it holds it fully and simultaneously believes against it. For Kierkegaard, the absurd is not a weakness in faith but its very structure.

cast.name: Abraham
cast.description: Not a tragic hero, not an ethical exemplar, but a singular figure who defies every category Johannes de Silentio can construct for him. He takes the three-day journey in silence, raises the knife in silence, and receives Isaac back in silence. He cannot speak because his absolute duty to God admits no translation into the universal language of ethics. He is, for Kierkegaard, the greatest human being who ever lived — and the most incomprehensible.

cast.name: Johannes de Silentio
cast.description: The narrator who writes the whole book from a position of admitted incapacity. He is not a knight of faith, cannot make the movement, and knows it. He circles Abraham with admiration, rewriting the story four different ways in the opening pages, and confesses again and again that he cannot understand what Abraham did. His inadequacy is not rhetorical humility — it is Kierkegaard's argument that faith cannot be approached from the outside, and that a philosopher who pretends otherwise is deceiving himself.

whyItMatters.title: What Faith Actually Requires
whyItMatters.body: The book asks whether faith is a comfort or a scandal. Kierkegaard's answer is the second. Real faith, he argues, asks the believer to stand alone before God in moments where every ethical principle says otherwise. The argument has unsettled Christian thought for nearly two centuries.

whyItMatters.title: The Knight of Faith
whyItMatters.body: Kierkegaard imagines Abraham not as a serene saint but as a man in agony, fully aware that what he is doing looks like murder. The image of the "knight of faith" — the believer who has accepted the absurd — is the founding image of Christian existentialism.

whyItMatters.title: The Limits of the Universal
whyItMatters.body: Kierkegaard argues that there are moments where the individual's relationship to God is higher than the universal moral law. The argument is dangerous and he knows it. He writes the book partly as a warning. The questions it raises — about authority, conscience, and the limits of ethics — remain open.
